prompt: The tree with no depth limit scores 1.000 on its training rows. What does that show?

choices.text: That it memorised them
choices.why: Right. Remembering rows is not learning about members.

choices.text: That it is the best of the six trees
choices.why: On the validation rows it is the worst, 0.636.

choices.text: That the training rows contain a leak of the label into the features
choices.why: No leak is needed: an unlimited tree can fit any rows perfectly.

choices.text: That AUC is the wrong score for trees
choices.why: AUC is fine; it was computed on the wrong rows.

prompt: Which maximum depth had the best validation AUC in overfit.py?
What does an AUC of 0.5 mean for the lapse model?

choices.text: Half the members are predicted to lapse
choices.why: AUC says nothing about how many are flagged.

choices.text: No better than a coin at ranking pairs
choices.why: Right. AUC is that pairwise chance, from 0.5 to 1.

choices.text: It is right about half the members and wrong about the rest
choices.why: That would be accuracy, not AUC, and lesson 4 shows why it misleads.

choices.text: The model was trained on half the rows
choices.why: AUC does not describe the training set.

prompt: Match each set to its job.

pairs.right: one honest estimate, at the end

prompt: After seeing a disappointing test score, a colleague tries another depth and checks the test again. What has happened?

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the test rows were not used for training
choices.why: They were used for choosing, which is a kind of learning.

choices.text: The model now overfits the training rows
choices.why: The problem is with the test rows, not the training rows.

choices.text: The test set became a validation set
choices.why: Right. There is no honest number left until fresh rows are held back.

choices.text: The score will be lower, because each look costs accuracy
choices.why: Looking costs nothing in the score; it costs its honesty.

prompt: In a platform, who should compute the score on the test rows?

choices.text: The person tuning the model, as often as they need
choices.why: Then the test rows become part of the tuning.

choices.text: Nobody: a held-out test is too small to matter
choices.why: 3,130 members is enough to tell 0.76 from 0.79.

choices.text: Whoever trained the previous version of the model
choices.why: Who it is matters less than that nobody choosing uses it.

choices.text: The release step
choices.why: Right. Training jobs do not read the test rows at all.

prompt: What is leakage?

choices.text: Information in the rows that will not exist when the model is used
choices.why: Right. Both scores look excellent, and production does something nobody measured.

choices.text: A test set smaller than the training set
choices.why: That is normal and harmless.

choices.text: Rows lost between the warehouse and the training job
choices.why: Losing rows is a different problem; leakage adds information.

choices.text: A model that leaks members' personal data in the predictions it serves
choices.why: That is a privacy problem; leakage here is about time.

prompt: For the lapse model, what is the moment of prediction?

choices.text: The day the member's 90-day window closes
choices.why: That is when the label becomes known, after the prediction.

choices.text: The cutoff, the night the scores are computed
choices.why: Right. What is known by then may be a feature.

choices.text: The member's first purchase
choices.why: That only starts their history.

choices.text: The day the model was trained, whenever that was
choices.why: A model trained once is used at many later cutoffs.

prompt: In leak.py, member 1's recency is -14 days. What does the negative value give away?

choices.text: That the member joined after the cutoff
choices.why: Joining is tenure; a negative recency is a visit after the cutoff.

choices.text: That the purchases table has a wrong date
choices.why: The date is right; it is read from the wrong moment.

choices.text: That they came back after the cutoff, which is the label itself
choices.why: Right. The model learned to read the answer.

choices.text: That pandas subtracted the dates in the wrong order
choices.why: The order is right; the later date is from after the cutoff.

prompt: Trained on the summary table and used in production, how many of 3,130 members did the model predict would lapse?
The leaky model still ranks members with AUC 0.787 in production. Why is it still unusable?

choices.text: Because 0.787 is below the 0.8 every model needs to reach production
choices.why: There is no such rule; the honest model scores 0.790 too.

choices.text: Because it was trained on fewer members than the honest one
choices.why: Both trained on the same members.

choices.text: Because the summary table is deleted every night
choices.why: It is rebuilt, and that is exactly why it only holds the present.

choices.text: Its probabilities are off by a factor of four
choices.why: Right. Any threshold, budget or forecast built on them is wrong.

prompt: What lets the platform compute a feature as it stood on a past cutoff?

choices.text: The history, or snapshots kept rather than overwritten
choices.why: Right. Lesson 6 builds the point-in-time join on top of that.

choices.text: Rebuilding the summary table more often
choices.why: More often still only holds the present.

choices.text: Dropping recency from the features altogether
choices.why: Recency is the most useful feature; it just has to be computed as of the cutoff.

choices.text: Training on the summary table but testing on purchases
choices.why: That is what production would do, and it gave 2,450 false alarms' worth of nonsense.

prompt: Why does a random split of nine stacked cutoffs flatter the model?

choices.text: Random splits always put the easier rows in the test set
choices.why: Chance has no preference for easy rows.

choices.text: The same members end up in training and test
choices.why: Right. The test is partly people the model met a month earlier or later.

choices.text: Nine cutoffs are too many rows for a random forest
choices.why: 25,000 rows is small for a forest.

choices.text: The newest cutoff's labels are unfinished
choices.why: The newest is 30 November, whose window closed on 28 February.

prompt: What AUC did the random split report in splits.py?
A model will score customers of a shop that opens next year and has never sold anything. Which split tests it honestly?

choices.text: A random split of rows, since the shop has no history
choices.why: That would test it on people it has already met.

choices.text: Training on the newest cutoff only
choices.why: Newness of the date does not make the people new.

choices.text: One that keeps whole members on one side
choices.why: Right. In production every customer is new, so the test has to be too.

choices.text: No split: score it on all the rows
choices.why: That is the score that lies.

prompt: Put these dates for the lapse model in calendar order.
items: the test labels are known, 28 February

prompt: For a model with a 90-day label window used on date T, the newest training cutoff is T minus ___ days or earlier.
A nightly job retrains the lapse model on every cutoff up to yesterday. What is wrong with its training set?

choices.text: Nothing: more recent rows are more relevant
choices.why: Recent, and with labels still being written.

choices.text: It has too many rows to train overnight
choices.why: Size is not the issue.

choices.text: It forgets the older cutoffs
choices.why: Every cutoff is in it; the newest ones are the problem.

choices.text: Its newest labels are still being written
choices.why: Right. Members with no time to return are counted as lapsed.

prompt: What share of members was labelled lapsed for the cutoff 2026-02-15, in percent?
Where does the fix for unfinished labels belong?

choices.text: In the pipeline that builds the training set
choices.why: Right. One condition: cutoff plus 90 days on or before the last complete day.

choices.text: In the modeller's notebook, as a filter before fitting
choices.why: It is a property of when the data landed, so it belongs where the data is built.

choices.text: In the model, which learns to ignore recent rows
choices.why: A model cannot tell an unfinished label from a real one.

choices.text: In the dashboard, which hides the newest cutoffs
choices.why: The damage is in the training, not in what anybody sees.

prompt: Which of these labels need a maturity before they can be trusted? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: a member lapsing within 90 days
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: a purchase returned within thirty days
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: a fraud reported by a chargeback
choices.why: Right. It can take weeks.

choices.text: the category of a book bought today
choices.why: That is known the moment it is bought.

prompt: Why does target encoding fitted on all rows leak so badly?

choices.text: It creates too many columns for the model
choices.why: It creates one column per category, not many.

choices.text: It writes the test rows' labels into their features
choices.why: Right. Each category becomes the average label, test rows included.

choices.text: It changes the order of the rows
choices.why: Order has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: Its averages are computed in floating point
choices.why: Precision is not the issue; what it averages is.

prompt: You are handed a model plus a separate scaler that was fitted in a notebook on the whole dataset. What is the risk for production?

choices.text: The scaler will be too slow at prediction time
choices.why: Applying a scaler costs nothing; the problem is how it was fitted.

choices.text: Scalers cannot be saved to a file next to the model
choices.why: They can; that is not the problem.

choices.text: It saw the test rows and lives outside the model
choices.why: Right. Inside a pipeline, fit fits both on the training rows only, the same way every time.

choices.text: It will reorder the categories of home_shop
choices.why: A scaler touches the numeric columns, not the categories.

prompt: A lapse model suddenly scores 0.994. What is the first suspect?

choices.text: The algorithm, which must be a better one
choices.why: Predicting people 90 days ahead is not that easy for any algorithm.

choices.text: The random seed
choices.why: A seed moves a score by a little, not to nearly perfect.

choices.text: The test set, which must be too small to trust
choices.why: A small set is noisy in both directions, not suspiciously perfect.

choices.text: The data
choices.why: Right. A score that good is a symptom: look for a leak.

prompt: A churn feature is called orders_total and comes from the customer summary rebuilt nightly. How would you check it for leakage in one query?

choices.text: Compare it with the orders on or before each row's cutoff
choices.why: Right. Any row where it is larger counts orders from the future.

choices.text: Count how many rows have a null orders_total
choices.why: Nulls are a different problem.

choices.text: Check that its average is the same in training and test
choices.why: A leaky column can have the same average in both.

choices.text: Drop it and see whether the score falls
choices.why: Any useful feature lowers the score when dropped; that proves nothing.

prompt: Which leak in this lesson is the one a data engineer causes most often?

choices.text: Overfitting a deep tree
choices.why: Overfitting is a modelling problem, and not a leak.

choices.text: A feature read from a table as it is today
choices.why: Right. Warehouse tables are built for the present.

choices.text: Looking at the test set twice
choices.why: That is the tuner's habit, not the platform's.

choices.text: Choosing four groups for k-means
choices.why: That is a choice, not a leak.
